jharkhand-public-health-workers-2500-doc.author: Aryaman Kumar
jharkhand-public-health-workers-2500-doc.core: Posted in last 7 days Jharkhand Public Health Workers - 2,500 Doctor Vacancies Impact Reading a vacancy number: what 2,500 empty doctor posts can tell you, and what they can't. A report on our site says more than 2,500 doctor posts in Jharkhand's hospitals, about 35 percent of the total, are vacant. The same report mentions preparations to recruit for more than a thousand third- and fourth-grade posts. A vacancy rate is easy to quote and hard to feel. In a district hospital, a vacant post can mean a department without a specialist, a clinic running fewer hours, or patients travelling to a bigger town for care that should have been available nearby. The number is a statewide figure. The experience is local, and it probably varies a great deal from one district to the next. What the figure doesn't tell us: which districts carry the biggest gaps, which specialities are missing, and how long the posts have been empty. A post vacant for a month and one vacant for five years are the same line in a spreadsheet and very different problems for the people who depend on that hospital. It also doesn't tell us how the recruitment plan relates to the doctor vacancies. Third- and fourth-grade posts keep hospitals running, and filling them matters, but they aren't a substitute for doctors. A drive that fills one category while the other stays open is only partial progress. So the questions worth following: how many of the doctor vacancies sit in the most remote districts, what the timeline is for filling them, and whether anyone publishes district-level numbers regularly instead of once in a while. Numbers like this are easy to scroll past. Behind the percentage is the distance someone travelled to see a doctor. If you work in or near Jharkhand's public health system and can tell us what these vacancies look like in your district, we'd like to hear from you. Still prototype. Still building — including the stories that start as a percentage. chronovissor.com #BuildingInPublic #Jharkhand Chronovissor

payroll-and-hris-analysts-combined-role-.headline: Payroll & HRIS Analysts - Combined Role Challenges & Pay Gaps
payroll-and-hris-analysts-combined-role-.author: Katrina Flowers, MSOP
payroll-and-hris-analysts-combined-role-.core: Posted in last 7 days Payroll & HRIS Analysts - Combined Role Challenges & Pay Gaps A job posting titled “Payroll and HRIS Analyst” is asking for two people and budgeting for one. I pulled 36 HRIS job postings from the last six months to see how often the role gets folded into another one. At larger employers, it was rare: 1 posting in 22. At employers under about 5,000 employees, it was 4 in 14, and payroll was the pairing almost every time. The pay told the rest of the story. The two combined payroll and HRIS analyst roles that listed pay had midpoints around $63,000 and $74,000, while the HRIS-only analyst roles sat at a median of about $102,000. It is a small sample, and the direction is hard to ignore. Payroll needs to spend its time understanding the payroll system, its trends and its changes: annual increases, escalated pay discrepancies, and deductions that shift every time benefits or tax rules change. HRIS needs to see all aspects of HR, with a close connection to the CHRO and the CHRO’s lens, and decide with IT how a tool like the pay system gets deployed to meet the CHRO’s goals for how pay is handled. Those two jobs look like a Venn diagram, with some slight overlap and definite differentiators, and the differentiators are why one person can’t be effective at both. Payroll is my example, and you can swap in benefits, recruiting or the HR generalist and the math stays the same. I understand why smaller organizations group the role, because when you don’t have large recruiting or training functions, combining looks efficient. Expect your payroll lead to know the system and manage it like a program, and still give the HRIS work its own owner. EVEN THE SALARY SHOULD NOT BE SHARED. Your auditors already agree with me on part of this, since segregation of duties guidance says the person who changes HR data shouldn’t also have access to the payroll system. A few questions worth asking before your next posting goes live: Does anyone on your team own HRIS as their whole job? When the payroll calendar and a system decision collide, which one wins? Who decides how your next pay tool gets deployed, and are they looking through the CHRO’s lens? I’m starting interviews to find out what is really happening inside these roles. If you hold a combined HRIS title, have hired for one, or have built or configured HR systems for a team where one person wears both hats, I want to hear from you. Comment INTERVIEW or send me a message. The title you post is the first design decision in your HR technology, and whatever you combine on the org chart, the system will combine too. __________________________________________________________________ I’m Katrina Flowers, an HR transformation and technology advisor who makes sure the HR process and the technology are built to fit each other, so the practitioners who run the process aren’t overworked and the system actually gets adopted. adults-who-overcame-addiction-and-trauma.author: Whitney Lavender ♿️🦿🤍
adults-who-overcame-addiction-and-trauma.core: Posted in last 7 days Adults Who Overcame Addiction & Trauma - Whit's Grit Podcast When I was a little girl, I used to tell people I was going to be a CNN anchorwoman. Why CNN specifically? I have no idea. 😂 It just stuck. Even then, I understood what a well-told story could do. I spent a lot of my childhood lost in books. When life got rough, books were where I could go to get away for a while. And there were more rough parts than I care to count or tell right now. I share pieces of my own story because I hope someone going through something similar might feel a little less alone. And somewhere along the way, I realized how much I love sitting across from someone and hearing their story. Whether I’m sitting down with a guest on Whit’s Grit or catching up with a fighter after a bout for MemphoWars, I’m reminded that everybody has a story. Sometimes all it takes is asking the right question and giving someone the time to answer it. I’ve heard stories of triumph, strength, resilience, heart, and grit. I’ve also heard people talk about heartache, brokenness, addiction, abuse, and trauma. Sometimes all of that lives in the same story. It’s an honor when someone trusts me with parts of their life that are hard to say out loud. I take that trust seriously, and I always want to do their story justice. If you’ve ever sat down with me and shared your heart, your passion, or a little of what makes you tick, thank you from the bottom of mine. That little girl who wanted to be a CNN anchorwoman would get such a kick out of what I get to do today. I really am living out a dream, and I’m grateful you’re part of it. 💜 I’ll be booking recordings for Whit’s Grit again soon. If we haven’t talked yet and there’s a story you’d like to share, shoot me an email. I’d love to hear from you. 📧 [email redacted] CNN
